A static library is copied into the executable while linking. A dynamic library (`.dll`, `.so`) is loaded when the program starts.

cards.q: Does CMake compile your code?
cards.a:
No, it generates build files for other tools

CMake describes the project and generates, for example, Ninja files or a Visual Studio solution. Those then run the compiler.

cards.q: The program builds but fails on start-up saying a DLL is missing. Which of the three requirements failed?
cards.a:
The run-time one: the DLL is not where it can be found

It built, so compiling and linking succeeded. Only the run-time search for the DLL failed.

cards.q: When is `T&&` a forwarding reference?
cards.a:
When `T` is deduced from that very parameter, or as `auto&&`

In `template <typename T> void f(T&& x)` it is a forwarding reference. In a member of `Box<T>` where `T` is already fixed, `T&&` is a plain rvalue reference.

cards.q: What is `T` deduced as when an lvalue `int` is passed to a `T&&` parameter?
cards.a:
`int&`

For an lvalue, `T` becomes `int&`, and `int& &&` collapses to `int&`. For an rvalue, `T` is plain `int`.

cards.q: Why is a named rvalue reference an lvalue?
cards.a:
A value category belongs to an expression, and a name refers to an object that can be used again

Inside the function, `x` can be used many times, so using its name is an lvalue expression. That is why you write `std::move(x)` or `std::forward<T>(x)`.

cards.q: What is the difference between `std::move` and `std::forward`?
cards.a:
`std::move` always gives an rvalue; `std::forward` keeps the caller's

`std::forward` restores the category the caller passed, which `T` recorded. `std::move` is unconditional.

cards.q: What is the difference between the `_v` and `_t` suffixes?
cards.a:
`_v` gives the trait's `value`; `_t` gives its `type`

`std::is_pointer_v<T>` is `std::is_pointer<T>::value`, and `std::remove_const_t<T>` is `typename std::remove_const<T>::type`.

cards.q: Why does `if constexpr` matter when using traits?
cards.a:
Branches not taken are not instantiated for this type

With a plain `if`, both branches must compile for every `T`, even the one that never runs.

cards.q: How is a trait such as `is_pointer` implemented?
cards.a:
A `false_type` primary template and a `true_type` one for `T*`

Pattern matching by specialization: `T*` matches the specialization, everything else gets the primary template.

cards.q: Why is `typename` needed in `typename RemoveConst<T>::type`?
cards.a:
The name depends on `T`, so it must be marked as a type

Until `T` is known, the compiler cannot tell whether `::type` is a type or a value. `typename` says it is a type.

cards.q: Is an error in the body of a function template subject to SFINAE?
cards.a:
No, an error in the body is a hard error

SFINAE applies to the immediate context: the signature, return type and template arguments. The body is too late.

cards.q: What does `std::declval<T>()` do?
cards.a:
It gives a `T&&` without building one, for `decltype` only

`decltype(std::declval<T>().size())` asks about `size()` even when `T` has no default constructor. Calling it for real is an error.

cards.q: How does `std::enable_if_t<false>` remove an overload?
cards.a:
It names a missing member type, so substitution fails

`std::enable_if<false>` has no `type` member, so substituting fails and overload resolution ignores that template.

cards.q: How does tag dispatch differ from SFINAE?
cards.a:
It removes nothing; normal overloading picks on a tag argument

A public function forwards to `impl(args, std::true_type{})` or `impl(args, std::false_type{})`, and normal overloading picks.

cards.q: What is the difference between a `constexpr` function and a `consteval` function?
cards.a:
Only a `consteval` function must run at compile time

`consteval` makes an "immediate function": every call must produce a constant, or the build fails.

cards.q: What does `constinit` add to a static variable?
cards.a:
Compile-time initialization, while staying modifiable

`constinit` avoids the static initialization order problem without making the variable read-only.

cards.q: Why can a `constexpr` function use a `std::vector` internally but not return one into a `constexpr` variable?
cards.a:
Compile-time allocations must be freed before evaluation ends

Compile-time allocation is allowed only if it is freed within the same evaluation, so the vector cannot survive into the program.

cards.q: What happens to undefined behaviour during constant evaluation?
cards.a:
The compiler diagnoses it as an error

Constant evaluation must be well defined, so overflow or out-of-bounds access there stops the build. This makes `constexpr` tests useful.

cards.q: Why can CRTP shapes of different types not be stored in one vector?
cards.a:
Each has a different base, so there is no common base

Static polymorphism gives every class its own base type. For a mixed collection you need virtual functions or a variant.

cards.q: What does CRTP use in place of the vtable?
cards.a:
A `static_cast` to the derived type, known when compiling

The base knows the derived type as its template argument, so `static_cast<Derived&>(*this)` calls it directly and can be inlined.

cards.q: Why does `Counted<T>` give each class its own counter?
cards.a:
Each `Counted<T>` is a distinct class with its own static

Each instantiation of the template is a separate class, so each gets its own copy of the static member.

cards.q: What does C++23's deducing `this` provide?
cards.a:
An explicit object parameter deduced as the real type

`void draw(this const auto& self)` sees the real derived type as `self`, which replaces many CRTP uses.

cards.q: How does type erasure differ from ordinary inheritance-based polymorphism?
cards.a:
The concrete types need no common base class at all

The virtual functions are still there, but hidden inside the wrapper. The user's types need no common base.

cards.q: Name two type-erased types in the standard library.
cards.a:
`std::function` and `std::any`

`std::function` holds any callable and `std::any` any copyable value. `std::variant` is a closed set of types, not type erasure.

cards.q: What is the small buffer optimization?
cards.a:
Storing small objects inside the wrapper, without the heap

If the object fits in a buffer inside the wrapper, it is constructed there instead of on the heap.

cards.q: Why can a type-erased wrapper have value semantics?
cards.a:
Copying clones the stored object through the hidden interface

A virtual `clone()` in the hidden interface lets the wrapper deep-copy without knowing the concrete type.

cards.q: What does `std::index_sequence_for<int, char, bool>` produce?
cards.a:
`std::index_sequence<0, 1, 2>`

It produces one index per type, starting at 0.

cards.q: Why do expression templates make vector arithmetic faster?
cards.a:
They fuse the expression into one loop, with no temporaries

`a + b + c` builds a lightweight expression object, evaluated element by element only when assigned.

cards.q: How does a metafunction return its result?
cards.a:
Through a nested member such as `type` or `value`

Templates compute with types, so the "result" is a nested member that the caller reads, such as `::type`.

cards.q: Why is `std::index_sequence` needed to iterate over a tuple?
cards.a:
`std::get<I>` needs each `I` as a compile-time constant

A run-time loop variable cannot be a template argument. A pack of indices expanded in a fold supplies each `I` while compiling.

cards.q: What happens if a joinable `std::thread` is destroyed?
cards.a:
`std::terminate` is called

A `std::thread` must be joined or detached before destruction. `std::jthread` joins automatically in its destructor.

cards.q: How do you pass an argument to a thread by reference?
cards.a:
Wrap it in `std::ref`, and ensure the object outlives the thread

The thread constructor copies its arguments. `std::ref(x)` passes a reference wrapper instead, and `x` must live long enough.

cards.q: Why is cancellation cooperative?
cards.a:
A thread killed mid-update could leave a lock held or data broken

`request_stop()` only sets a flag. The thread checks its `std::stop_token` and finishes cleanly.

cards.q: Why is `parallelSum` free of data races?
cards.a:
No thread writes anything that another thread reads or writes

Sharing read-only data and writing to separate elements needs no locks. The results are combined after the threads join.

cards.q: What is a data race?
cards.a:
Unsynchronized access to one variable, with at least one write

Data races are undefined behaviour. Concurrent reads alone are fine; a write without synchronization is not.

cards.q: How does `std::scoped_lock` prevent deadlock with several mutexes?
cards.a:
It locks them all together with a deadlock-avoiding algorithm

Two threads listing the same mutexes in different orders cannot deadlock, because `std::scoped_lock` never holds one while waiting forever for another.

cards.q: Why is calling `lock()` and `unlock()` directly dangerous?
cards.a:
An exception or early return between them leaves the mutex locked permanently

RAII locks such as `std::lock_guard` and `std::scoped_lock` unlock in their destructor on every path.

cards.q: Why does making every member function thread-safe not make every use of the class safe?
cards.a:
Another thread can act between two separate calls

`if (!q.empty()) q.pop();` can fail if another thread pops in between. Offer a combined `tryPop()` instead.

cards.q: Why must `wait` be given a `std::unique_lock` and not a `std::lock_guard`?
cards.a:
`wait` must unlock and relock it, which `lock_guard` cannot

`std::lock_guard` has no `unlock()`. A `std::unique_lock` can be unlocked and relocked by `wait`.
cards.lessonTitle: Condition Variables, Semaphores, Latches and Barriers

cards.q: What is the difference between a latch and a barrier?
cards.a:
A latch counts down once and cannot be reused; a barrier resets after each phase

Use a latch for "wait until N things are ready" once, and a barrier for threads that meet at the end of every round.
cards.lessonTitle: Condition Variables, Semaphores, Latches and Barriers

cards.q: Why always wait with a predicate?
cards.a:
Spurious wake-ups and early notifications are then harmless

`cv.wait(lock, [&] { return ready; })` rechecks the real condition, so stray wake-ups and early notifications are harmless.
cards.lessonTitle: Condition Variables, Semaphores, Latches and Barriers

cards.q: How does a semaphore differ from a mutex?
cards.a:
It allows up to N holders, and any thread may release a permit

A counting semaphore limits access to N, such as at most four downloads. A mutex has one owner who must unlock it.
cards.lessonTitle: Condition Variables, Semaphores, Latches and Barriers

cards.q: What happens to an exception thrown inside a `std::async` task?
cards.a:
It is stored and rethrown when `get()` is called

The future carries either the result or the exception, so the caller handles it as if the call were local.
cards.lessonTitle: Futures, Promises, std::async and Thread Pools

cards.q: Why state `std::launch::async` explicitly?
cards.a:
The default policy may defer the task, so nothing runs in parallel

With the default policy, the task may run lazily on the thread that calls `get()`. `std::launch::async` forces a new thread.
cards.lessonTitle: Futures, Promises, std::async and Thread Pools

cards.q: Why must the future returned by `std::async` be kept?
cards.a:
Its destructor waits for the task, so a discarded future makes the call synchronous

The temporary future is destroyed at the end of the statement and blocks there until the task is finished.
cards.lessonTitle: Futures, Promises, std::async and Thread Pools

cards.q: In the thread pool, why is the vector of workers the last member?
cards.a:
Destroyed first, the workers are joined while the queue still exists

The workers use the queue and the mutex. Declaring them last means they are destroyed first, while the others still exist.
cards.lessonTitle: Futures, Promises, std::async and Thread Pools

cards.q: Does making two variables atomic make `if (a) { b = 1; }` thread-safe?
cards.a:
No; each operation is atomic, but the combination is not

Another thread can change `a` between the test and the write. Use a mutex or a compare-exchange design for the whole step.

cards.q: What does a release store paired with an acquire load guarantee?
cards.a:
Writes before the release are visible after the acquire reads it

Release/acquire publishes data: write the data, then release-store a flag; a thread that acquire-loads the flag sees the data.

cards.q: What is false sharing?
cards.a:
Threads writing separate variables that share one cache line

The variables are independent, but the hardware shares cache lines. Padding or `alignas(64)` separates them.

cards.q: Why is `volatile` not a substitute for `std::atomic`?
cards.a:
It gives neither atomicity nor ordering between threads

`volatile` is for memory-mapped hardware. Threads need `std::atomic` or a mutex.

cards.q: Why may a function run under `par_unseq` not lock a mutex?
cards.a:
Interleaved iterations on one thread could deadlock on it

Vectorized iterations may run interleaved on one thread, so taking a lock could deadlock against itself.

cards.q: Why use `std::reduce` instead of `std::accumulate` for parallel work?
cards.a:
`reduce` may regroup the operations; `accumulate` may not

Regrouping requires an associative, commutative operation. For floating point, results can differ slightly.

cards.q: What is wrong with incrementing a captured counter inside a parallel `for_each`?
cards.a:
It is a data race on the counter

Many threads write the same `int` at once. Let the algorithm do the combining, or use an atomic.

cards.q: What does Amdahl's law say?
cards.a:
The sequential part of the work limits the speed-up

If 10% is sequential, no number of cores can make the program more than 10 times faster.

cards.q: What makes a function a coroutine?
cards.a:
Using `co_await`, `co_yield` or `co_return` in its body

The body decides: any of the three `co_` keywords turns the function into a coroutine. The return type must then support it.

cards.q: Why should coroutine parameters usually be taken by value?
cards.a:
It may resume after the caller's objects are destroyed

Parameters are copied into the coroutine frame. A reference parameter would still point at the caller's object, which may be gone.

cards.q: What is the role of the promise type?
cards.a:
Its members define how the coroutine starts, yields and returns

The compiler calls the promise's members, such as `initial_suspend` and `yield_value`, at each step of the coroutine's life.

cards.q: Why can one thread serve thousands of suspended coroutines?
cards.a:
A suspended coroutine occupies no thread, only a small frame

Unlike a blocked thread, a suspended coroutine has no stack of its own, just its frame, so very many are cheap.

cards.q: Why can undefined behaviour affect code that runs *before* the faulty operation?
cards.a:
The optimizer assumes the undefined behaviour never happens

The compiler reasons "this path would be UB, so it cannot happen" and may remove or rearrange earlier code on that basis.

cards.q: What is the safe way to reinterpret a `float`'s bits as an integer?
cards.a:
`std::bit_cast<std::uint32_t>(f)`, or `std::memcpy` before C++20

`reinterpret_cast` through a pointer breaks strict aliasing and the union trick is UB in C++. `static_cast` converts the value, not the bits.

cards.q: What does the strict aliasing rule allow the compiler to assume?
cards.a:
That pointers to unrelated types do not refer to the same object

A write through a `float*` cannot change an `int`, so the compiler may keep the `int` in a register. (`char` and `std::byte` are the exceptions that may alias anything.)

cards.q: When does a temporary's lifetime get extended?
cards.a:
When it is bound directly to a `const` reference or an rvalue reference

It then lives as long as that reference. Binding through a function's returned reference does not extend it.

cards.q: Why does a struct holding a `char` followed by a `double` occupy 16 bytes?
cards.a:
The `double` needs 8-byte alignment, so 7 bytes of padding follow

1 byte of `char`, 7 of padding, then 8 of `double`: 16 in total.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Layout, Alignment, Unions and Bit Fields

cards.q: In C++, may you read a union member other than the one last written?
cards.a:
No, it is undefined behaviour; use `std::bit_cast`

Only the last-written member is active. C allows type punning through unions; C++ does not.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Layout, Alignment, Unions and Bit Fields

cards.q: Why is there padding at the end of a struct?
cards.a:
So each element of an array of the struct stays aligned

In an array, each element starts where the previous one ends, so the size must keep the next element aligned.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Layout, Alignment, Unions and Bit Fields

cards.q: Why are bit fields unsuitable for portable file formats?
cards.a:
Their order and packing differ between compilers

Two compilers may lay the same bit fields out differently. Use shifts and masks on a fixed-width integer for file formats.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Layout, Alignment, Unions and Bit Fields

cards.q: What does placement new do?
cards.a:
It constructs an object in existing memory, allocating nothing

`new (buffer) T{ ... }` only runs the constructor. You must later call the destructor yourself and release the memory separately.
cards.lessonTitle: Custom Memory: Placement new, Allocators and PMR

cards.q: Why is a monotonic buffer so fast?
cards.a:
Allocating bumps a pointer, and freeing does nothing

It never tracks individual frees, which is perfect for short-lived bursts of allocations.
cards.lessonTitle: Custom Memory: Placement new, Allocators and PMR

cards.q: Why can two `std::pmr::vector<int>` with different resources be passed to the same function?
cards.a:
The resource is a run-time pointer, not part of the type

Classic allocators are template arguments and change the type. A pmr container holds a `std::pmr::memory_resource*` instead.
cards.lessonTitle: Custom Memory: Placement new, Allocators and PMR

cards.q: Why must a memory resource outlive the containers that use it?
cards.a:
The containers use it until they are destroyed themselves

Destroying the resource first leaves the containers with a dangling pointer for their final deallocation.
cards.lessonTitle: Custom Memory: Placement new, Allocators and PMR

cards.q: What is a cache line, and why does it matter?
cards.a:
The 64-byte unit memory moves in; in-order access uses all of it

Memory arrives a cache line at a time. Walking through memory in order uses every byte fetched; jumping around wastes most of each line.

cards.q: When is a struct of arrays the better layout?
cards.a:
When loops use one or two fields of many objects

Keeping each field in its own array means a loop over positions reads only positions, with no other fields filling the cache.

cards.q: Why can sorting data make a loop with a condition faster?
cards.a:
The branch becomes predictable, so the processor stops mispredicting it

With sorted data, the condition is false for a long run and then true for a long run, which the branch predictor learns.

cards.q: What should you do before optimizing anything?
cards.a:
Profile a Release build to find where the time is actually spent

Guesses about performance are usually wrong. Measure optimized code, then fix the parts that really dominate.

cards.q: What does `export` do in a module?
cards.a:
It makes a declaration visible to the module's importers

Only exported declarations are seen by importers. Unexported helpers are invisible outside the module.

cards.q: Do macros defined in a module affect its importers?
cards.a:
No, modules do not export macros

Importing a module never brings in its macros, which is one of the ways modules are cleaner than headers.

cards.q: Why are modules faster to build than headers?
cards.a:
Its interface is compiled once, not re-parsed per file

Each `#include` pastes and re-parses the header text. An `import` loads an already compiled interface.

cards.q: What is the global module fragment for?
cards.a:
Including ordinary headers before the module declaration

It starts with `module;` and holds `#include` lines whose contents should not become part of the module.

cards.q: Why does `SQUARE(i++)` misbehave?
cards.a:
The text `i++` appears twice, so `i` changes twice

A macro is text substitution: `((i++) * (i++))`. A `constexpr` function would evaluate its argument once.
cards.lessonTitle: Preprocessor Deep Dive, Attributes and User-Defined Literals

cards.q: What does `[[nodiscard]]` do?
cards.a:
The compiler warns if the return value is ignored

Use it on functions whose result matters, such as error codes, so ignoring the result is flagged.
cards.lessonTitle: Preprocessor Deep Dive, Attributes and User-Defined Literals

cards.q: How does `std::source_location::current()` as a default argument report the caller's location?
cards.a:
Default arguments are evaluated where the call is

The default argument is evaluated where the call is written, which gives the caller's file and line.
cards.lessonTitle: Preprocessor Deep Dive, Attributes and User-Defined Literals

cards.q: What job can only the preprocessor do?
cards.a:
Choosing between code that cannot all compile together

`constexpr` and templates replace most macros, but `#if` is still needed to choose code that would not even compile on other platforms.
cards.lessonTitle: Preprocessor Deep Dive, Attributes and User-Defined Literals

cards.q: Why does `std::cout << "hi"` work without writing `std::operator<<`?
cards.a:
Argument-dependent lookup searches `std`, home of `cout`'s type

ADL looks in the namespaces of the arguments' types, so it finds the `operator<<` declared in `std`.
cards.lessonTitle: Name Lookup, ADL, Inline Namespaces and the ODR

cards.q: What makes violations of the One Definition Rule so dangerous?
cards.a:
They are usually not diagnosed at all

Two different definitions with the same name in different files can silently pick either one, with no error.
cards.lessonTitle: Name Lookup, ADL, Inline Namespaces and the ODR

cards.q: Why write `using std::swap;` before an unqualified `swap(a, b)`?
cards.a:
`std::swap` becomes a fallback while ADL can find a better one

This "two-step" lets a type's own efficient `swap` win when it exists, and uses `std::swap` when it does not.
cards.lessonTitle: Name Lookup, ADL, Inline Namespaces and the ODR

cards.q: How can a hidden friend be found?
cards.a:
Only through argument-dependent lookup

A friend defined inside the class is not visible to normal lookup. That keeps overload sets small and avoids surprises.
cards.lessonTitle: Name Lookup, ADL, Inline Namespaces and the ODR

cards.q: Why must the destructor of a pImpl class be defined in the source file?
cards.a:
Deleting `Impl` needs its full definition, found only there

Defining the destructor (even as `= default`) in the `.cpp`, after `Impl` is defined, lets `unique_ptr` delete it.

cards.q: What is the modern C++ alternative to the classic Visitor pattern?
cards.a:
`std::variant` with `std::visit`

A variant of the node types plus `std::visit` handles each type, with the compiler checking every case is covered.

cards.q: What are the costs of pImpl?
cards.a:
A heap allocation per object and an extra indirection

In exchange you get a stable header and faster rebuilds, since private changes no longer recompile users.

cards.q: Why is a singleton discouraged?
cards.a:
It is a global in disguise that hides dependencies

Code that reaches for `Logger::instance()` hides that it needs a logger. Passing the dependency in makes it visible and replaceable.

cards.q: Which sanitizer finds data races?
cards.a:
ThreadSanitizer

ThreadSanitizer (`-fsanitize=thread`) tracks accesses from different threads. AddressSanitizer finds memory errors such as use-after-free.
cards.lessonTitle: Testing, Sanitizers, Static Analysis and Tooling

cards.q: What is the difference between static analysis and a sanitizer?
cards.a:
Static analysis needs no run; a sanitizer checks while running

They complement each other: analysers find problems in code that never runs in tests; sanitizers catch real failures in code that does.
cards.lessonTitle: Testing, Sanitizers, Static Analysis and Tooling

cards.q: Why does high coverage not prove the tests are good?
cards.a:
It shows code ran, not that a bug there would be caught

A test with no checks can still run every line. Coverage finds untested code; it does not measure the checks.
cards.lessonTitle: Testing, Sanitizers, Static Analysis and Tooling

cards.q: What does a data breakpoint do?
cards.a:
It pauses the program when a particular variable's value changes

Data breakpoints (watchpoints) find the code that modifies a variable unexpectedly.
cards.lessonTitle: Testing, Sanitizers, Static Analysis and Tooling

cards.q: Which standard is the start of "modern C++"?
cards.a:
C++11

C++11 added `auto`, lambdas, move semantics, smart pointers and much else, changing how C++ is written.
cards.lessonTitle: C++ Standards Timeline and Where to Go Next

cards.q: Why might a feature in the current standard be unavailable to you?
cards.a:
A feature can be used only when both your compiler and its standard library have implemented it

Implementations catch up over time. Check your compiler's support tables before relying on a new feature.
cards.lessonTitle: C++ Standards Timeline and Where to Go Next

cards.q: What is the modern replacement for `new` and `delete` in ordinary code?
cards.a:
`std::make_unique` and the standard containers

Owning objects through `std::unique_ptr` and containers removes manual `delete`, and with it leaks and double frees.
cards.lessonTitle: C++ Standards Timeline and Where to Go Next

cards.q: How often is a new C++ standard published?
cards.a:
Every three years

C++11, 14, 17, 20 and 23 followed a three-year cycle, with C++26 next.
cards.lessonTitle: C++ Standards Timeline and Where to Go Next
